glm2api · repository dissection

three reference projects, compared feature by feature

Each project turns a chat account into an OpenAI-style API. They differ in language, protocols, account handling and how they get captcha/device tokens. Read as source; nothing here was run.

use the bar above to go back

The one-line answer to "why three?"

They are three generations of the same idea the person described: D3-vin's is the fullest server (three API protocols, account pool, proxy rotation), pingmike2's is a smaller single-binary port of it for a VPS, and chaoticmindv's is a Node version that replaces the whole captcha-and-token problem with a real browser. No single one has everything; that is exactly what your new project can fix.

D3-vin / GLM-ZAI-2API

Go · internal/app · 27 files
Gomost complete
What it has
  • Three API protocols — OpenAI, Anthropic and Responses
  • Vision (GLM-5v-Turbo) and a tool-calling adapter with six parsing strategies
  • Browser TLS fingerprint (Chrome via tls-client) on every upstream request
  • Account pool from a token file, checked at startup, rotated on USER_BLOCKED, with guest fallback
  • WAF proxy rotation with a 10-minute dead-proxy timeout
  • In-process captcha — device-data built with two AES passes ported from the Aliyun widget
  • A separate Playwright token collector binary
What's lacking
  • No partner-facing page — token gathering is a side binary, not something a partner opens and leaves running
  • Captcha is solved in-process, so no human is in the loop when the challenge changes
  • Everything runs on one machine: no way for partners to contribute their own egress

pingmike2 / zai2api

Go · flat layout · 20 files
Gosimpler
What it has
  • Single binary meant to be dropped on a VPS, with a web dashboard
  • OpenAI-compatible /v1 endpoints with tool calling
  • SQLite device-token store taken oldest-first and deleted after use (a simple queue)
  • In-process captcha: build args → track hash → compress → encrypt → verify, returning a base64 param
  • Token pool with explicit batch/target/low-water numbers (150 / 750 / 50)
  • One static proxy for the WAF, with notes on datacenter IPs being rejected
What's lacking
  • Only the OpenAI protocol — no Anthropic, no Responses, no vision
  • No account pool and no guest fallback: the simpler token path of its parent is gone
  • Proxy is one fixed address, not a rotating pool — a single point of failure
  • No partner page and no browser-based collection, so it inherits the captcha fragility

chaoticmindv / zai2api

Node.js · 19 files
Nodereal browser
What it has
  • One-click Windows start — the easiest of the three to actually run
  • OpenAI-compatible endpoints with streaming; GLM's thinking passed through as reasoning_content
  • Same Aliyun captcha constants and flow as the Go projects
  • Playwright collector: drives a real browser, triggers the captcha by sending a message, waits for the token to appear, then harvests tokens in batches into SQLite
  • A background worker that re-checks the pool every 60 s while under target, every 10 min when full
What's lacking
  • Needs a full browser install per machine — heavy, and awkward to run headless on a server
  • No account pool and no proxy rotation at all
  • Only the OpenAI protocol
  • The collector is still a single browser on the operator's machine, not many partners

Read from each project's source in this workspace. "yes" is a feature found in the code, "part" means present but limited, "no" means not found — not found is not proof it is absent everywhere.

What this rebuild does NOT do yet

"Not done" means one specific step is unproven — not that the code is missing or broken. Every item below is written down for the same reason: a claim nobody checked is worse than an honest blank. Each one names the single thing that would close it.

  • A server now exists — one Node process, no dependencies, with real sessions, a key-gated mint socket, an even spread of work across partners, a token pool that expires and refills, and donation checking. What is still unproven is a live upstream call: nobody supplied a credential, so chat answers 501 with its reason instead of inventing a reply. Close it by setting GLM_UPSTREAM.
  • No real captcha mint has been observed. The widget is now configured from the hub's /config (env-driven, with the captured values as defaults), so it loads the real SDK whenever a hub answers. But minting happens in a partner's browser against the live site, and no browser with a screen has run it here. Close it by opening the minter tab on a machine that can reach chat.z.ai.
  • Nothing spends a held token. Donations arrive, get checked against Aliyun, and expire on a timer — but the only thing that would spend one is a working upstream, which is the first gap.
  • No Tor yet. It appears as an egress class in the admin panel, but there is no SOCKS5 client or circuit rotation behind it, so no traffic is routed through a volunteer's connection.

Read the three projects above as design input, not as code to copy: what they solved (protocols, token queues, proxy rotation) tells you what this server should grow next.

What none of them has (your gap)

  • A partner page. All three gather tokens on the operator's own machine. Your minter page inverts that: partners open a page, keep it in a tab, and their browsers solve captchas and donate egress — no shared secret, no installed software.
  • Spread-out rate limits. None of them paces requests across several egress points; they either use one proxy or a pool of proxies the operator owns.
  • Two token sources. The person wants partners to contribute from either chat.z.ai or chatglm.cn; all three hard-code one upstream.
  • An honest consent surface. The minter page states plainly what runs in the partner's browser — the three projects have no such page.
